blocks.text: Photosynthesis uses light energy that is absorbed and converted into chemical energy by photosynthetic pigments. In plants it can be summarised as: 6CO2 + 12H2O + light gives C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Carbon dioxide, water and light are the reactants; glucose and oxygen are the products. Water appears on both sides because it is used as a reactant in some reactions and released as a product in others, but there is no net yield of water.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: Photosynthesis is the process in which the energy-poor inorganic compound of carbon (CO2) is reduced to energy-rich carbohydrates. Plants convert only about 1 to 2 percent of the solar energy they receive into chemical energy, yet this is enough to sustain almost all life on Earth.

blocks.title: Compensation point
blocks.text: Photosynthesis uses the products of respiration and respiration uses the products of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis occurs only in daylight, but respiration goes on day and night. At dawn and dusk, when light is low, the rates of photosynthesis and respiration may be equal for a short time: the oxygen released by photosynthesis just equals what respiration needs, and the carbon dioxide released by respiration just equals what the photosynthesising cells need, so there is no net gas exchange between the leaves and the atmosphere. This is the compensation point. At noon photosynthesis outruns respiration, so there is a net release of oxygen and uptake of carbon dioxide.
Role of light

Light provides the energy that drives the chemical reactions transforming simple molecules into complex organic compounds. Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and converted into chemical energy, which is stored in organic compounds as the energy of C-H bonds.
Action spectrum

Photosynthetic pigments absorb different wavelengths of light at different rates, and the different wavelengths are also differently effective in photosynthesis. The effectiveness of each wavelength is determined as the action spectrum: a plant is illuminated with different colours of light one by one, and for each colour the rate of photosynthesis is measured by the amount of oxygen emitted from the leaves; the data are plotted as the action spectrum. The first action spectrum was made by the German biologist T. W. Engelmann in 1883, working on the photosynthetic pigments of Spirogyra. When the cells of a filament were illuminated with different wavelengths, maximum photosynthesis occurred in the cells receiving blue and red light, so these emitted the most oxygen.
Role of carbon dioxide

Sugar is formed by the reduction of CO2 using ATP and NADPH, so CO2 is the source of carbon for making sugars. Carbon dioxide enters the leaves through the stomata and dissolves in the water absorbed by the cell walls of the mesophyll cells. Stomata are found in large numbers in leaves, and the entry of CO2 depends on their opening.

blocks.title: Where photosynthesis happens
blocks.text: About 10 percent of total photosynthesis is carried out by terrestrial plants; the rest occurs in oceans, lakes and ponds. Aquatic photosynthetic organisms use dissolved CO2, bicarbonates and soluble carbonates as their carbon source; land plants use atmospheric CO2.
Role of water

Water is the source of hydrogen for the reduction of CO2 during photosynthesis. The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from water, so water is an important source of the atmospheric oxygen that most organisms need for aerobic respiration. In the 1930s Van Niel hypothesised that the plant splits water as a source of hydrogen, releasing oxygen as a by-product; his hypothesis was based on photosynthetic bacteria that make carbohydrate from carbon dioxide without releasing oxygen. It was confirmed in the 1940s by an experiment with the isotopic tracer of oxygen, 18O.

blocks.alt: Two plants. Group 1 plants get water with heavy oxygen, H2(18)O, and ordinary CO2, and release heavy oxygen, (18)O2. Group 2 plants get ordinary water and C(18)O2, and release ordinary O2. Below, the two equations: 6CO2 + 12H2(18)O gives C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6(18)O2; and 6C(18)O2 + 12H2O gives C6H12(18)O6 + 6H2(18)O + 6O2, with the heavy oxygen atoms coloured.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3: Experiment to prove that water is the source of oxygen released in photosynthesis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3).

blocks.text: In photosynthesis water is split to release hydrogen. This hydrogen reduces the coenzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) to NADPH, and the reduced coenzyme NADPH serves as the reducing power for the reduction of CO2 to form sugar.
Role of photosynthetic pigments

Photosynthetic pigments are present in the thylakoid membranes, where they capture the light energy necessary for photosynthesis. They include chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenes, and different pigments absorb light of different wavelengths (colours). Light behaves like a stream of particles called photons, and a pigment molecule absorbs one photon at a time. When a pigment molecule absorbs a photon, its electrons move to a higher energy level, so it becomes energy-rich, or excited.

blocks.title: Photon energy
blocks.text: Short-wavelength photons (blue) have higher energy than long-wavelength (red) photons. More energetic photons promote electrons to higher energy levels.
Chlorophylls

Chlorophyll is a lipid molecule. Chlorophylls a, b, c and d are found in plants and algae, while the others, the bacteriochlorophylls, are found in photosynthetic bacteria. A chlorophyll molecule has two parts, a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail. The head is a porphyrin ring of four pyrrole rings (five-sided nitrogen-containing compounds) held together by a magnesium atom in the centre; in chlorophyll a the second pyrrole ring carries a methyl (CH3) group, in chlorophyll b an aldehyde (CHO) group at the same spot. The porphyrin ring absorbs light. The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain that anchors the molecule in the thylakoid membrane. Chlorophylls absorb mainly violet-blue and orange-red wavelengths; green is least absorbed and is transmitted or reflected.

blocks.alt: A porphyrin ring of four pyrrole rings, each with a nitrogen atom bonded to a central magnesium atom. Side groups: a vinyl group (H2C=CH) and CH3 on ring I, R and CH2-CH3 on ring II, CH3 on ring III, H3C on ring IV, and a fifth ring with C=O carrying a COOCH3 group. A CH2-CH2 chain from ring IV ends in an ester group joined to a long hydrocarbon chain. Key: R = CH3 in chlorophyll a; R = CHO in chlorophyll b. Labels: Porphyrin ring (Hydrophilic head), Hydrocarbon chain (Hydrophobic tail).

blocks.text: Accessory pigments

Accessory pigments are all the pigments other than chlorophyll a that gather light for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment, and the others are the carotenoids (carotenes and xanthophylls) and the phycobilins. Chlorophyll b and the carotenoids are found in plants; phycobilins are found in red algae and cyanobacteria. When accessory pigments absorb light they pass the energy on towards chlorophyll a. Some wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll a are absorbed very effectively by chlorophyll b and vice versa, so the two together absorb a wider range of light.

blocks.title: Carotenoids
blocks.text: Carotenoids such as beta-carotene play a dual role: they capture light energy in the blue and green regions of the spectrum and protect the photosynthetic apparatus from damage by excess light.
Absorption spectrum

A graph showing the different wavelengths absorbed by a pigment is its absorption spectrum. The absorption spectrum of the chlorophylls shows that absorption of blue light (430 nm) and red light (670 nm) is maximum, while the absorption peaks of the carotenoids are different. The action spectrum of photosynthesis also shows that blue and red light are the most effective, so the action spectrum of photosynthesis coincides with the absorption spectrum of the photosynthetic pigments.

blocks.alt: Two graphs over a coloured spectrum background, wavelength 350 to 700 nm. (a) Absorption of light: chlorophyll-a (solid) peaks near 430 and 662 nm, chlorophyll-b (dashed) near 453 and 642 nm, carotenoids (dotted) between about 420 and 480 nm, with a legend. (b) Photosynthesis rate / absorption rate: the action spectrum (black curve) is high in blue and red and low in green; the absorption spectrum (grey area) lies under it with matching blue and red peaks.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.5: (a) Absorption spectrum; (b) Action spectrum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.5).

blocks.text: Organisation of photosynthetic pigments: photosystems

For efficient absorption and use of solar energy, the photosynthetic pigments are organised into clusters called photosystems, embedded in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts. Photosystems contain the photosynthetic pigments and the carriers of the electron transport chain. Each photosystem consists of a light-gathering antenna complex and a reaction centre. The antenna complex has many pigment molecules that capture light energy and pass the excitation energy, as high-energy electrons, to the reaction centre. The reaction centre has one or more molecules of chlorophyll a, which pass the high-energy electrons to a primary electron acceptor; the acceptor passes them on to the series of electron carriers collectively called the electron transport chain.

blocks.alt: An oval chloroplast in long section with an outer membrane and an inner membrane around the stroma. Inside, six stacks of disc-shaped thylakoids (grana) are joined by thin lamellae. Labels: Outer membrane, Inner membrane, Stroma, Thylakoid, Granum (a bracket around one stack), Lamella.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.6: Structure of Chloroplast (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.6).

blocks.text: In the chloroplast there are two photosystems, photosystem I (PS-I) and photosystem II (PS-II), named in order of their discovery. PS-I has the P700 chlorophyll a molecule in its reaction centre and absorbs light of 700 nm best; the reaction centre of PS-II has P680 chlorophyll a, which absorbs light of 680 nm best.

blocks.alt: A cluster of green pigment molecules of the antenna with a darker reaction center in the middle. Photons fall on the antenna; curved arrows pass the energy through the pigments to the reaction center; a large arrow carries 2e- from the reaction center up to the primary electron acceptor. Labels: Photons, Pigment molecules of antenna, Reaction center, 2e-, Primary electron acceptor.

blocks.text: Mechanism of photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is a redox (oxidation-reduction) process. When water molecules are split they are oxidised, losing electrons and hydrogen ions, and yield oxygen; meanwhile CO2 is reduced to sugar as electrons and hydrogen ions are added to it. Oxidation and reduction go hand in hand. It is not a single-step process but a complex metabolic pathway of many reactions. The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana, and the light-independent reactions in the stroma of the chloroplast.

blocks.alt: A chloroplast with a granum on the left labelled Light Dependent Reactions (in grana) and a circular arrow in the stroma on the right labelled Light Independent Reactions (in stroma). Light and H2O enter the light-dependent reactions and O2 leaves; CO2 enters the light-independent reactions and Sugar leaves. ATP and NADPH pass from the grana to the stroma; ADP + Pi and NADP+ return.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.8: Overview of photosynthesis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.8).

blocks.text: 1. Light-dependent reactions

The key events of the light-dependent reactions are the absorption of light energy by the photosynthetic pigments, the excitation of electrons by that energy, and the formation of ATP and NADPH. The formation of ATP is the most important step and is called photophosphorylation; it is either non-cyclic or cyclic.

blocks.title: Reducing and assimilating powers
blocks.text: During the light-dependent reactions light energy is absorbed and converted into chemical energy in the form of reducing and assimilating powers, NADPH and ATP. The light-independent reactions use NADPH and ATP to reduce CO2 and so store chemical energy as C-H bond energy.
a) Non-cyclic photophosphorylation
This is the usual way ATP is produced in the light-dependent reactions. Both photosystems take part and two electron chains are involved.

items: Absorption of light by PS-II: when light falls on PS-II, the energy level of the chlorophyll molecules of its antenna rises. Two excited electrons move from them, pass between chlorophyll molecules and reach the P680 chlorophyll in the reaction centre. With this energy boost, P680's two excited electrons pass to the primary electron acceptor of PS-II, creating an electron hole in P680, which becomes a strong oxidising agent.

Photolysis of water: the electron hole is filled by electrons from water. When a water molecule reacts with the oxidised chlorophyll of PS-II it breaks into two hydrogen ions, an oxygen atom (which immediately combines with another to form O2) and two electrons, which fill the hole in P680. This water-splitting step is photolysis.

Electron flow from PS-II to PS-I: the photoexcited electrons received by the primary acceptor of PS-II now pass to PS-I through the electron transport chain of PS-II, whose carriers are plastoquinone (PQ), the cytochrome complex and plastocyanin (PC). As the electrons move down the chain their energy decreases and is used by the thylakoid membrane to produce ATP by chemiosmosis.

Absorption of light by PS-I: light energy absorbed by PS-I boosts its chlorophyll molecules to a very high level; the excited electrons of the P700 chlorophyll of its reaction centre pass to the primary electron acceptor of PS-I, and the electrons coming from PS-II fill the hole in P700.

Electron flow from PS-I to NADP+: the primary acceptor of PS-I passes the photoexcited electrons to a second electron transport chain, where they are received by ferredoxin (FD). The enzyme NADP reductase transfers them from FD to NADP+; when NADP+ gets two electrons and an H+ ion it is reduced to NADPH, which stores the high-energy electrons.

blocks.alt: Photons fall on the antenna of PHOTOSYSTEM II; energy reaches P680, and 2e- go up to its primary electron acceptor. Water splits: H2O gives 2H+, half O2 and 2e-, and the 2e- refill P680. From the acceptor 2e- pass down through PQ, the cytochrome complex and PC to P700 of PHOTOSYSTEM I; an orange wedge beside this chain is labelled Energy for synthesis of ATP by chemiosmosis.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.9: Light-dependent reactions (noncyclic photophosphorylation) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.9).
blocks.long_description: Photons fall on the antenna of PHOTOSYSTEM II; energy reaches P680, and 2e- go up to its primary electron acceptor. Water splits: H2O gives 2H+, half O2 and 2e-, and the 2e- refill P680. From the acceptor 2e- pass down through PQ, the cytochrome complex and PC to P700 of PHOTOSYSTEM I; an orange wedge beside this chain is labelled Energy for synthesis of ATP by chemiosmosis. Photons on PHOTOSYSTEM I send 2e- from P700 up to a second primary electron acceptor, then to FD; the 2e- and H+ convert NADP+ to NADPH.

blocks.text: So light energy is converted into chemical energy in ATP and NADPH. The zigzag path taken by the electrons through PS-II, PS-I and the electron transport chains is called the Z-scheme.

blocks.title: Atmospheric oxygen
blocks.text: The oxygen produced during photolysis is the main source of atmospheric oxygen.
b) Cyclic photophosphorylation

Under certain conditions the photoexcited electrons of PS-I take an alternative path, cyclic electron flow, which uses PS-I but not PS-II. The electrons cycle back from the primary electron acceptor of PS-I to the P700 chlorophyll through the electron transport chain. There is no production of NADPH and no release of oxygen, but the cyclic flow generates ATP. It happens when the Calvin cycle slows down and NADPH accumulates in the chloroplast.

blocks.alt: PHOTOSYSTEM I alone: photons fall on its antenna, energy reaches P700, and 2e- go up to the primary electron acceptor. A dashed arrow takes the 2e- back to the cytochrome complex, which also receives 2e- from PQ; from the cytochrome complex 2e- pass to PC and back to P700. An orange wedge beside the chain is labelled Energy for synthesis of ATP by chemiosmosis.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.10: Cyclic Photophosphorylation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.10).

blocks.text: Chemiosmosis

During the light-dependent reactions, as electrons are transferred along the series of carriers of the electron transport chain, oxidation and reduction reactions occur: a carrier is oxidised when it loses electrons and the next carrier is reduced when it gains them. The electrons lose energy during this carrier-to-carrier transport, and chemiosmosis is the mechanism by which the thylakoid membranes couple these redox reactions to the synthesis of ATP.

The energy released from the electrons is spent on the active transport of H+ ions from the stroma of the chloroplast into the inner compartment of the thylakoid (the lumen), so many H+ ions are deposited in the lumen. This H+ gradient has potential energy. The H+ ions diffuse back from the lumen into the stroma, from higher to lower concentration, passing through a special protein of the thylakoid membrane, the enzyme ATP synthase. This enzyme uses the energy yielded by the flow of H+ ions to make a bond between ADP and inorganic phosphate, so ADP is converted into ATP and the energy is packed into it.

blocks.alt: An inset chloroplast labelled Thylakoid and Stroma points to a section of thylakoid membrane between the thylakoid lumen (top) and the stroma (bottom). In the membrane: PS II, electron carriers, PS I and ATP synthase. Light falls on PS II and PS I. In the lumen H2O splits into 2H+ and half O2, giving 2e-. A yellow path carries the electrons through the carriers and PS I to the stroma, where NADP+ + H+ become NADPH.

blocks.text: 2. Light-independent reactions

The light-independent reactions are a series of reactions in the stroma of the chloroplast that use carbon from CO2, energy from ATP and hydrogen ions from NADPH to construct energy-rich sugar molecules. They are also called the dark reactions, because they can occur in the absence as well as the presence of light as long as ATP and NADPH are available. Their details were discovered by Melvin Calvin and his colleagues at the University of California, so they are also called the Calvin cycle; Calvin was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1961 for this work. The Calvin cycle has three phases.
Phase I: carbon fixation

Carbon fixation is the initial incorporation of CO2 into organic material. The enzyme ribulose biphosphate carboxylase (rubisco, probably the most abundant protein on Earth) combines three molecules of CO2 with three molecules of the five-carbon sugar ribulose biphosphate (RuBP). This gives six molecules of the three-carbon compound 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA), or 3-phosphoglycerate. Because the product of the initial fixation is a three-carbon compound, the Calvin cycle is also known as the C-3 pathway.

blocks.alt: A cycle of carbon-bead boxes around CALVIN CYCLE. Phase I, Carbon Fixation: 3 CO2 join 3 ribulose biphosphate (RuBP) with Rubisco, giving 6 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA). Phase II, Reduction: 6 ATP give 6 ADP and the 3-PGA becomes 6 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid; 6 NADPH give 6 NADP+, 6 P leave, and 6 glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) form. One G3P leaves for glucose and other compounds. Phase III, Regeneration of RuBP: 5 G3P lose 2 P and use 3 ATP (giving 3 ADP) to remake 3 RuBP.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.12: The Calvin cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 5.12 points the 6 ATP and 6 NADPH arrows towards ATP and NADPH, as if they were produced, and prints '1,3-Biphsophoglyceric acid'. In this step ATP and NADPH are used up (ATP to ADP, NADPH to NADP+), and the name is 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid, as drawn above.
Phase II: reduction

Six phosphate groups are taken from six ATPs and added to the molecules of 3-PGA, so each 3-PGA becomes 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid. Each of these is then reduced to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P), NADPH providing the hydrogen for the reduction, and phosphate groups are also detached. Six molecules of G3P are produced, of which one leaves the cycle; it combines with another G3P to make glucose, which may then be converted into other carbohydrates.

blocks.title: G3P again
blocks.text: G3P is the same three-carbon sugar that is formed in glycolysis, the first phase of cellular respiration, by the splitting of glucose.
Phase III: regeneration of RuBP

Through a series of reactions, five molecules of G3P are converted into three molecules of ribulose phosphate (RuP). One phosphate group is added to each RuP, using three ATPs from the light reactions, to make three molecules of RuBP. These RuBP receive CO2 again and the cycle continues.
